The 58-year-old Silver City Restaurant (銀都冰室) recently posted a "glorious closure" notice at its premises, stating that they have walked together through 58 years of ups and downs, expressing gratitude for the generous support over the years, and deep regret for being unable to bid farewell earlier, with a heart full of reluctance. The shop has been gradually packing up and clearing out in recent days, with the signage and marble slabs at the entrance having been removed. Over the past few days, many regular customers and neighbourhood residents have stopped by the shop to chat and say goodbye to the proprietress and the staff, and to take photos as mementos.

Many regular customers and neighbourhood residents have stopped by the shop to chat and say goodbye to the proprietress and the staff.

Eighty-year-old original resident: They are friends, not customers

80-year-old Mrs. Fung (馮婆婆), upon seeing the boss, immediately greeted him warmly and chatted cheerfully. Mrs. Fung moved in when Wah Fu Estate (華富邨) was first built, and has lived there for nearly 60 years. Having watched Silver City Restaurant pass from the first-generation Mr. and Mrs. Yuen (阮氏夫婦) to the second-generation daughter, and now seeing it close with glory, she said, "Of course I can't bear to see it go. I'm so happy coming down here, hahaha. I've watched them grow up for decades, watched them study, watched them get married."

Helping to clear up when staff are busy

She used to visit occasionally, but since retiring in recent years, she has come almost every morning for a meal, becoming close with the staff and the boss. Each morning, she would read newspapers and magazines, play with her phone, chat for a while, laugh a bit, and then leave. "We became like good friends. Going in, we'd laugh and joke. Basically, it's the friend kind, not the customer kind." Sometimes, when she saw the staff were busy, she would voluntarily help clear the bowls and plates and wipe the tables after eating, "so that when people come, there's a table for them to sit at." When the staff had their meals, she didn't mind sitting with them, and they knew she wasn't a picky eater, so they generously gave her the staff meals and leftover dishes.

"In life, people come together and part ways"

Facing the parting, Mrs. Fung said what she will miss most is this friendship, but she also understands that the boss needs a day of rest, and redevelopment is a wheel that cannot be stopped. "I tell myself not to be too sad. In life, people come together and part ways. We're already very lucky to have been together for so many years."

Mrs. Fung's unit faces the sea, and she candidly says she likes this home. "If it weren't good, I wouldn't have lived here so long. I moved in and I'll stay until they demolish it." However, she said she takes a very philosophical view of things: "Since that's how it is, are you going to lie down on the ground and protest? That's the government's policy. Are the buildings really that structurally sound?" Mrs. Fung's unit is not expected to be vacated until after 2030, and she joked that at her age, "We'll deal with it when the time comes... No matter how long they take to build (the new estate), I don't know if I'll even be able to see it when it's finished."

Youth who grew up in Wah Fu Estate: Losing a habit

26-year-old Ah Ching has lived in Wah Fu Estate since birth, and he says he really likes cha chaan tengs and ice rooms, often visiting Wah Fu Ice Room (華富冰室) and Silver City Restaurant in the estate. Upon learning of Silver City's closure in the early hours of August 1, he felt distressed and suffered insomnia that night, candidly saying he has lost a place that gave him a sense of security. The place is full of Ah Ching's memories: for example, over a decade ago, he often ate there with a bus driver friend, who has since passed away. Last year, he also brought a Japanese friend to the shop, and his friend was amazed that such an old establishment had customers of different ages, and highly praised the red bean ice there. Sadly, before he could visit again, Silver City has already closed.

(Provided by interviewee Ah Ching)

Ah Ching said the cha chaan teng has a lot of his "comfort food," like toast and milk tea, and in the ice room, from choosing a seat after entering, to the waiter bringing tea, and him ordering, every part of it was a place that made him feel safe and secure when he was emotionally unstable. "They have a way of making you feel taken care of." He especially liked sitting by the window at Silver City Restaurant, unhurried, looking out at the podium of Wah Fu Shopping Centre (華富商場) opposite and the blue sky. "Just looking at this scene like this is already so blissful."

Losing Silver City Restaurant, Ah Ching said, is losing a habit and a last sanctuary. "When they (traditional ice rooms) disappear one by one, where can I still go?... I really don't know where I can go." With Wah Fu's redevelopment, the gradual departure of old shops is foreseeable, and Ah Ching described it as a very helpless acceptance: "Is it really the case that if I say I can't bear to part with this place, they won't demolish it? Of course not." But he feels that people are free, and since they don't want to forget, "You have your own way, you can choose to remember them."

Only about one-third of shops in Wah On House (華安樓) still in operation

As for the first phase of redevelopment, which is divided into two parts, in Phase 1a, residents of Wah On House and Wah Lok House will choose flats this month, and are expected to begin moving into units on Wah King Street (華景街) between October and November, with all residents required to move out by the end of July next year. Phase 1b, comprising Wah Cheong, Wah Tai, and Wah Kin Houses, as well as the reception estates Wah Lok Path (華樂徑) and Wah Fu North Estate (華富北邨), are expected to see move-ins in 2028 and 2030 respectively, with the goal of full clearance by March 2031.

As the first batch of affected buildings, most of the ground-floor shops in Wah On House have already pulled down their shutters and closed, with only about one-third still in operation. These include "Lai Wah Salon" (麗華髮廊), "Wah Cheong Store" (華昌士多), "Golden Crown Snacks" (金冠零食), "Pak Tat Laundry" (百達洗衣), and "Kam Kee Cart Noodles" (鑑記車仔麵), all long-established shops, which are expected to continue operating until they are required to vacate.

As for whether they will move to the new reception estates to continue operating, some shops said they are still considering. A staff member of Golden Crown Snacks said that if the Housing Department can arrange a shop for them, they should hopefully continue operating. The seventy-year-old boss of Wah Cheong Store, Mr. Chan, however, is worried that they will have to move into a shopping centre in the future, with high rent and reduced foot traffic, making business difficult. He expects the over-40-year-old store to end with the demolition of Wah On House: "Retire, won't do it anymore."
